problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?

activity_context.topic_title: Surface Areas of Revolution: Rotation About the X-Axis

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}}$ that lies in the first quadrant between the line $y=0$ and its $y$-intercept. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =2 \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\sqrt{2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{\frac{2}{2-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{y}{\sqrt{2-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
